message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This study is built on a six-month pilot with 4,000 households across three deliberately mixed wards, so the projections are based on how Thornbury residents actually behave, not national averages. We measured participation and tonnage weekly, by housing type, and the results are encouraging: strong participation, consistent yields and 81% of residents rating the service good or very good. Crucially, participation held up across houses and flats, which means we can roll out a single, simple service across the district rather than designing separate arrangements. The financial analysis is complete and transparent. Every cost line is shown, from vehicles to liners, and the disposal saving uses our actual incineration cost and Brookfield's quoted gate fee, giving a net cost of about £490,000 that is fully covered by the provisional new-burdens allocation. Treatment is local, at a plant 14 miles away. The timetable works back from the vehicle lead time. I am confident the Council can approve this roll-out knowing it is evidence-based and fully funded.
</author>

Your review is being evaluated on whether it identifies the problems in the document.

<document>
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection feasibility study

The recommendation that the service is "evidence-based and fully funded" is not supported by the document. The problems below are in rough order of importance.

## Major problems

**1. Participation is not "broadly similar" across housing types.**
Table 1 shows 66% for houses and 21% for flats, a threefold gap. The text and the author's summary ("participation held up across houses and flats") contradict the study's own table. The case for a single uniform service has no support. Flats probably need a different approach, such as communal bins or different caddies and communications. The study doesn't cost or design that approach.

**2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't achieve.**
Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate", but Table 1 gives 57% overall. The pilot's flat share (20%) matches the district's (20%), so 57% is the right blended figure: 0.8×66% + 0.2×21% = 57%.
- 52,000 × 0.64 × 1.9 kg × 52 weeks gives the stated 3,290 t.
- At 57% the figure is about 2,900 t, roughly 12% lower.
- The 64% figure appears nowhere in the evidence. It overstates tonnage and the disposal saving.

**3. Treatment capacity doesn't cover the projected tonnage.**
Brookfield offers up to 1,800 t/year until 2029, against 3,290 t projected (about 2,900 t on the corrected figure). Roughly 1,100–1,500 t has no secured outlet except a plant 46 miles away.
- Neither that plant's gate fee nor the extra haulage cost is given.
- The £74/t saving is therefore only established for 1,800 t, or about £133,000 a year, not £243,000.
- "Treatment is local, 14 miles away" is true only for part of the waste.
- The capacity shortfall is mentioned in Section 4 but never carried into the costs or recommendation.

**4. "Fully funded" is overstated, and the margin is thin or negative.**
- The £520,000 is a provisional allocation, and the Government has only "indicated" funding. It isn't confirmed, yet the study asks Cabinet to authorise the vehicle order.
- The arithmetic (£733,400 − £243,000 ≈ £490,000) is correct. But on the corrected tonnage (~2,900 t, saving ~£217,000) the net cost is about £517,000, which uses up nearly all the allocation.
- Capping Brookfield at 1,800 t and paying more for the rest would push the cost past £520,000.
- There is no sensitivity analysis or contingency.

**5. The cost analysis is not "complete".** It omits or glosses over:
- The £990,000 vehicle capital outlay, which appears only as depreciation, so there is no cash or financing view.
- The cost of longer haulage to a second plant.
- Supervision, management and depot costs, and staff on-costs, leave cover and agency cover.
- Inflation and gate-fee escalation after the Brookfield contract.
- Any offsetting saving from reduced residual rounds.
- Whether six vehicles and crews can serve 52,000 households, with no round design shown.
- The basis for the £88,000 line, since liners are an ongoing cost and the three-month initial supply is only part of it.

## Other issues

**6. Weak satisfaction evidence.** The 81% comes from "surveyed" households. There is no response rate, and non-participants (43% of the pilot) are probably under-represented. There is no breakdown by housing type, though flats are where the service performed worst.

**7. The pilot may not generalise.**
- The wards were selected, not random.
- The pilot ran for six months, with no data on participation trends over time despite weekly measurement. "Consistent yields" and "held up" are asserted, not shown.
- Pilot households got free liners and novelty effects. District-wide supply and sustained engagement may differ.

**8. The timetable has no float.**
- Vehicles ordered by December 2026 arrive in March 2027, the same month as caddy delivery and crew training, with collections starting 5 April.
- The vehicle lead time is never stated, even though the author says the timetable is built from it.
- Any delay in delivery means no trained crews and a missed start.
- A December order also depends on a Cabinet decision and funding that aren't yet confirmed.

**9. The legal basis needs checking.** The study says councils "are required" to introduce weekly collections but gives no date. As I understand it, the statutory deadline for most English councils was 31 March 2026. If so, an April 2027 start is late, and the study should say whether Thornbury has a transitional exemption.

## Suggested fixes before going to Cabinet
- Correct the projection to the observed 57%, or justify any higher figure.
- Redesign or separately cost the service for flats.
- Secure or cost the additional treatment capacity.
- Add sensitivity scenarios for participation, gate fees and funding.
- Include capital, overheads and contingency.
- Make the vehicle order conditional on confirmed funding.
- State the vehicle lead time and add schedule float.
